body.statement: Along \((P_\varepsilon)\) under SDC, the arm-\(1\) closure is \([3/5,4/5]\) at \(\varepsilon=0\) and \([3/10+\varepsilon/4,3/10+\varepsilon]\cup[3/5+\varepsilon/2,4/5+\varepsilon/4]\) for \(0<\varepsilon<3/110\). The arm-\(0\) closure is \([1/4,3/4]\), so the ATE closures are \([-3/20,11/20]\) at zero and \([-9/20+\varepsilon/4,11/20+\varepsilon/4]\) for positive \(\varepsilon\). Both set maps are Hausdorff-discontinuous at zero. For every \(q\in\{\mathrm{arm},\mathrm{ATE}\}\) and every positive \(\varepsilon_n=o(1/n)\), \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\widehat I_n}\max_{P\in\{P_0,P_{\varepsilon_n}\}}\mathbb E_{P^n}[\rho_H(\widehat I_n,\mathcal I_{\partial,q}(P))]\ge3/20\), where the infimum is over measurable nonempty compact-set estimators. This claim is SDC-only and makes no LEI boundary assertion.
body.justification: The theorem exposes the statistical cost of treating exact support eligibility as a discontinuous branch decision.
body.gap: Generic LP nonregularity is known, but the cited literature does not give this legal SDC family, the exact set jump, or the \(3/20\) minimax constant.
body.consumer: Inference procedures for the exact set can be screened against an explicit impossibility benchmark instead of promising uniform shrinking at zero slack.
body.proof_tex:
The beta-integral identities give mean \(9/10\) for \(\operatorname{Beta}(9,1)\), and mean \(3/10\) and variance
\[
 v_0=\frac{3\cdot7}{(3+7)^2(3+7+1)}=\frac{21}{1100}                            \tag{22}
\]
for \(\operatorname{Beta}(3,7)\).  Since \(\mathbb E_0[Y-3/10]=0\), the tilted density integrates to one, and
\[
 \mathbb E_\varepsilon[Y]
 =\frac{3}{10}+\frac{\varepsilon}{v_0}\mathbb E_0[Y(Y-3/10)]
 =\frac{3}{10}+\varepsilon.                                                     \tag{23}
\]
For \(|\varepsilon|<3/110\), the smallest possible value of the bracket in the density is positive: when \(\varepsilon<0\), it is bounded below by
\(1-|\varepsilon|(7/10)/v_0>0\), and when \(\varepsilon>0\), by
\(1-\varepsilon(3/10)/v_0>0\).  Hence every tilted factual law has topological support \([0,1]\).

The three cell masses give \(\mu_D=\mu_Z=1/2\).  Let \(x\in[0,1]\) be the missing mean for arm one in cell \((0,0)\).  Direct summation using (23) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \theta_1&=\frac{3}{10}+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}+\frac{x}{2},\\
 \operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,D)&=\frac{3}{20}+\frac{\varepsilon}{8}-\frac{x}{4},\\
 \operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Z)&=\frac{3\varepsilon}{8}-\frac{x}{4}.
 \end{aligned}                                                                 \tag{24}
\]
For \(0<\varepsilon<3/110\), the positive SDC branch in (24) is
\[
 0\le x\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{2},qquad
 \tau_{1,+}^{\mathrm{SDC}}(P_\varepsilon)=\frac{3\varepsilon}{2},             \tag{25}
\]
where the slack identity follows because \(3\varepsilon/2<1/2\).  Its arm-mean interval is
\([3/10+\varepsilon/4,3/10+\varepsilon]\).  The negative branch is
\[
 \frac35+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\le x\le1,qquad
 \tau_{1,-}^{\mathrm{SDC}}(P_\varepsilon)=\frac25-\frac{\varepsilon}{2},       \tag{26}
\]
and its arm-mean interval is
\([3/5+\varepsilon/2,4/5+\varepsilon/4]\).  At \(\varepsilon=0\), the positive branch is the singleton box vertex \(x=0\), so its slack is zero and \(\text{thm:support-eligibility}\) removes it; the negative branch remains \([3/5,4/5]\).  Equations (25)--(26) prove the asserted arm-one closures.

For arm zero, write \(u,v\in[0,1]\) for its missing means in cells \((1,0)\) and \((1,2)\).  The observed uniform cell has mean \(1/2\), and another direct summation gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \theta_0&=\frac14+\frac{u}{4}+\frac{v}{4},\\
 \operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,D)&=-\frac18+\frac{u}{8}+\frac{v}{8},\\
 \operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Z)&=-\frac18-\frac{u}{8}+\frac{3v}{8}.
 \end{aligned}                                                                 \tag{27}
\]
The positive branch has \(u+v\ge1\) and \(3v-u\ge1\), so its linear mean image is \([1/2,3/4]\); the endpoints are attained at \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((1,1)\).  The negative branch has the reversed inequalities and mean image \([1/4,1/2]\), attained at \((0,0)\) and \((1/2,1/2)\).  Both branch polytopes contain the interior vector \((1/2,1/2)\), so both are support-eligible.  Thus
\[
 \mathcal I_0^{\mathrm{SDC}}(P_\varepsilon)=[1/4,3/4]                           \tag{28}
\]
for all perturbations under consideration.  Uniform missing kernels for arm zero and the conditional product construction in \(\text{prop:ate-product-coupling}\) also verify simultaneous compatibility of both arms.

At zero, subtracting (28) from \([3/5,4/5]\) gives
\[
 \mathcal I_\Delta^{\mathrm{SDC}}(P_0)=[-3/20,11/20].                          \tag{29}
\]
For positive \(\varepsilon\), the two arm-one component differences are
\[
 [-9/20+\varepsilon/4,\ 1/20+\varepsilon]
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 [-3/20+\varepsilon/2,\ 11/20+\varepsilon/4].                                 \tag{30}
\]
They overlap because \(-3/20+\varepsilon/2\le1/20+\varepsilon\), so their union is the interval asserted in the theorem.

Let \(I_{q,0}=\mathcal I_{\partial,q}(P_0)\) and \(I_{q,\varepsilon}=\mathcal I_{\partial,q}(P_\varepsilon)\).  For the arm map, the low component in (25) lies below \(3/5\), and its left endpoint is farthest from \([3/5,4/5]\); the shifted high component has endpoint displacements at most \(\varepsilon/2\).  Therefore
\[
 d_H(I_{\mathrm{arm},0},I_{\mathrm{arm},\varepsilon})
 =\frac{3}{10}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.                                         \tag{31}
\]
For the ATE map, (29)--(30) are intervals whose lower endpoints differ by \(3/10-\varepsilon/4\) and whose upper endpoints differ by \(\varepsilon/4\), so (31) holds with \(\mathrm{arm}\) replaced by \(\mathrm{ATE}\).  Thus both set maps are Hausdorff-discontinuous at zero.

Only the cell \((D,Z)=(1,2)\), of probability \(1/4\), changes with \(\varepsilon\).  The definition of total variation and the tilted density give
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_\varepsilon,P_0)
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{8v_0}\mathbb E_0[|Y-3/10|]
 \le\frac{\varepsilon}{8\sqrt{v_0}},                                          \tag{32}
\]
where Cauchy--Schwarz and (22) give the inequality.  To verify the product bound directly, dominate both one-observation laws by a common measure, write their densities as \(p\) and \(q\), and use
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^np_i-\prod_{i=1}^nq_i
 =\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\prod_{k<i}p_k\right)(p_i-q_i)
                    \left(\prod_{k>i}q_k\right).
\]
Taking one half of the integrated absolute value gives
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_\varepsilon^n,P_0^n)
 \le n\operatorname{TV}(P_\varepsilon,P_0).                                   \tag{33}
\]
For completeness, we now prove the two-point decision inequality.  If \(Q_0,Q_1\) have densities \(q_0,q_1\) with respect to a common dominating measure, let \(\nu\) have density \(q_0\wedge q_1\); then \(\nu(\Omega)=1-\operatorname{TV}(Q_0,Q_1)\).  Since \(\rho_H=1\wedge d_H\) is a metric, every compact-set estimate \(\widehat I\) satisfies
\[
 \rho_H(\widehat I,I_0)+\rho_H(\widehat I,I_1)\ge\rho_H(I_0,I_1).
\]
Integration with respect to \(\nu\), followed by domination by \(Q_0\) and \(Q_1\), yields
\[
 \max_{i=0,1}\mathbb E_{Q_i}\rho_H(\widehat I,I_i)
 \ge \frac{\rho_H(I_0,I_1)}{2}\{1-\operatorname{TV}(Q_0,Q_1)\}.             \tag{34}
\]
Take \(Q_0=P_0^n\), \(Q_1=P_{\varepsilon_n}^n\).  The support restriction on \(\varepsilon_n\) holds eventually, (31) converges to \(3/10\), and (32)--(33) converge to zero because \(n\varepsilon_n\to0\).  Inequality (34) holds for every measurable estimator, so taking first the infimum over estimators and then the lower limit proves the constant \(3/20\) for both choices of \(q\).  Every step used only SDC; no LEI boundary conclusion is drawn.
